title: Issues: baseline and detail change, trading and swarming
blurb: Classify an issue, decide whether a change touches the baseline and who decides, and apply trading or swarming at team level.
question: Pinewick's marketing director asks for a Must have feature that is not in the project backlog. Is this a baseline change or a detail change, who decides, and what would trading or swarming do here?

teach.body: The issues practice collects and assesses issues and controls changes to the project's baseline. Agile delivery produces many product versions, so change is inevitable and should be embraced and supported, not resisted. The control point is the project backlog: a change that alters it is a change to the project baseline and is handled formally. A change that leaves it untouched is detail, handled informally by the team.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Pinewick's click and collect
teach.body: The marketing director asks for a new 'gift card collection' epic as a Must have for Release 2. It would change the project backlog, so project manager Patrick Dunne logs it in the issue register and writes an issue report for the board. Separately, the e-commerce team wants to show collection slot times, a story within an existing epic. Product owner Anita Shah agrees to swap out a Could have of similar effort. When a payment test environment fails, the team swarms on it and fixes it within a day.

teach.text: Traps: a change that alters the project backlog is a baseline change and goes formal, even if the team calls it a Must have. Trading swaps items of similar effort to absorb change; it is not how blockers are cleared. Swarming clears blockers; escalate an issue to the PM only if the team cannot resolve it, and treat it as an exception only when a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.

items: Issue types: request for change, off-specification, problem, business opportunity.
Changes the project backlog = baseline change: formal, board or delegated change authority.
Project backlog untouched = detail change: informal, at team level, seen as positive.
Issue register records formal issues; the issue report gives impact, options, recommendation.
Trading swaps equal-effort items with the PO; swarming puts the team on a blocker first.

summary: You can now classify an issue, decide whether a change touches the project baseline, and say who decides and where it is recorded. You can also apply trading to absorb change and swarming to clear blockers before escalating.

A.q: Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares project is in its second delivery stage. The government adds a contract condition that season ticket holders must also receive automatic compensation. This is not in the project backlog and would need a new Must have epic. How should this request be handled?
options: Informally, traded into a sprint by the product owner
As a new risk, recorded in the risk register
Formally, as a change to the project baseline
Through the next Agilometer assessment review
A.why: A new Must have requirement that changes the project backlog is a change to the project baseline; it needs formal handling and a decision by the project board or delegated change authority (11.3.1, 11.3.2).

whyNot.0: Trading at team level is for changes within the project backlog; a new Must have epic changes the baseline.
whyNot.1: The request has already arisen, so it is an issue (a request for change), not an uncertain future event.
whyNot.3: The Agilometer assesses the risks of agile working; it does not decide change requests.

A.q: During a sprint, Pinewick's e-commerce team learns that customers need to see collection slot times, a story within an existing epic. Product owner Anita Shah agrees with the team to drop a lower-priority 'gift wrap option' story of similar size so the new story fits. Which technique is being used?
A.why: Trading, or swapping, replaces one or more requirements with others of similar effort, agreed with the PO, so the change is absorbed without growing scope (11.4.1).

whyNot.0: Swarming focuses the whole team on a stuck task or blocker; here requirements are being swapped.
whyNot.2: Refactoring improves a product's internal structure without changing its behaviour.
whyNot.3: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, so there is no exception; the change is absorbed in the team.

A.q: Draycott's software team cannot get sensor data into the platform because of a gateway fault, which is holding up two stories. The whole team pauses its other work and tackles the fault together until it is fixed. Which technique is the team using?
A.why: Swarming is when the team focuses together on a problem or blocker that hinders progress; it is particularly effective for resolving issues (11.4.2).

whyNot.0: Trading swaps requirements of similar effort to absorb change; it does not clear a blocker.
whyNot.1: The team is resolving the blocker itself; escalation to the PM comes only if it cannot.
whyNot.2: A detail change is a change to requirements within the project backlog, not a team tackling a fault.

B.q: Easterholm County Council's supplier, Abacus Care Software, tells the project that its interface will not be able to pass assessment data in the format the specification requires. Which type of issue is this?
B.why: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its quality specification (11.3.1).

whyNot.0: A request for change is a proposal to change a baseline; here a product will fall short of its specification.
whyNot.2: A business opportunity is an unexpected positive consequence, which this is not.
whyNot.3: A problem is something with an immediate negative impact, such as supplier failure; this is a product that will miss its specification.

B.q: Partway through Callowmere University's project, the university's digital fund unexpectedly offers extra money that could pay for a Welsh-language version of the hub. Which type of issue is this?
B.why: A business opportunity is an unanticipated positive consequence, such as extra funding becoming available (11.3.1).

whyNot.1: Nothing is failing to meet its specification.
whyNot.2: A request for change proposes changing a baseline; this is new funding that creates a positive option.
whyNot.3: A problem has an immediate negative impact; this offer is positive.

B.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's chief executive asks for tenant-chosen appointment slots to be brought forward from Release 3 to Release 2, which would change the project backlog. The change can be made within the stage's tolerances. Which artifact should set out its impact on the baseline, the options and a recommendation for the decision?
B.why: An issue report describes an issue's impacts on the baseline, the options and a recommended decision (11.3.4).

whyNot.0: An exception report is used when a plan is forecast to exceed tolerance, which is not the case here.
whyNot.1: The issue register records the issue; the analysis and recommendation go in the issue report.
whyNot.2: The approach sets out how issues are handled, not the analysis of one particular change.

C.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's marketing director asks for a new 'gift card collection' feature, which she says is a Must have for Release 2. It is not in the project backlog. Product owner Anita Shah adds it to the e-commerce product backlog and swaps out two Could have stories of similar effort, without telling anyone else. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
options: Yes, because trading keeps the iteration's scope level
Yes, because the product owner owns the product backlog
No, because new requirements wait for the next release
No, because a project backlog change needs formal handling
C.why: A new Must have requirement that changes the project backlog is a change to the project baseline; it needs formal handling and a decision by the board or delegated change authority (11.3.1, 11.3.2).

whyNot.0: Trading does keep workload level, but it is for changes within the project backlog, not new baseline items.
whyNot.1: The PO owns the product backlog, but that does not give authority over changes to the project baseline.
whyNot.2: Change is embraced in agile; the issue is that this change needs formal handling, not that it must wait.

C.q: During a sprint, Draycott's tester finds that the alert service keeps failing, blocking three stories. The software team swarms on the fault for a day, fixes it and carries on without involving the project manager. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
options: Yes, because swarming is tried before escalating
Yes, because trading keeps the workload balanced
No, because blockers are raised as exceptions
No, because the PM should assign one person to it
C.why: Swarming is an effective issue resolution technique when a team meets a blocker; the team escalates to the PM as an issue only if it cannot resolve it (11.4.2).

whyNot.1: Trading swaps requirements to absorb change; it does not explain clearing a blocker.
whyNot.2: An exception arises when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; a blocker fixed in a day is not one.
whyNot.3: Agile teams self-manage how they tackle blockers; the whole team swarming is the recommended approach.

C.q: Callowmere University's wellbeing staff ask for clearer wording in the appointment confirmation message. The change does not affect the project backlog. Product owner Rebecca Lyle agrees, and the team swaps out a story of similar effort so the sprint stays on track. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the board delegated all changes to the PO
Yes, because detail changes are handled at team level
No, because every change needs a formal request for change
No, because wording changes need the CPO's decision
C.why: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change, seen as making the product more accurate, and handled informally at team level, here by trading with the PO (11.3.2, 11.4.1).

whyNot.0: Nothing says the board delegated all changes to the PO; the change is informal because it is a detail change.
whyNot.2: Formal handling is for changes to the project baseline; detail changes are handled informally.
whyNot.3: Detail changes inside the backlog are agreed at team level with the PO; the CPO need not decide.

reteach.title: Changing a wedding plan
reteach.question: A couple has a fixed budget and date for their wedding. Which changes can the planner sort out on the day, and which need the couple to decide?

blocks.h: Inside the plan or outside it?
blocks.body: Swapping the starter for another dish of the same cost is a detail: the planner sorts it out. Adding an evening fireworks show was never in the agreed plan, so the couple must decide formally. If the caterer's van breaks down, the whole team pitches in to fix it first. Only if they cannot fix it do they call the couple.

head: Wedding
PRINCE2 Agile
rows: Swap a dish of the same cost
Call the couple if still stuck

blocks.text: Calling a new item 'essential' does not let the planner add it on the day. If it changes the agreed plan, the couple decides.

explain.h: The project backlog is the line
explain.body: Ask one question: does the change alter the project backlog? Yes means a baseline change, handled formally. No means a detail change, handled informally by the team.

test.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's service design team wants to reorder the questions in the online repair form after tenant testing. The change does not affect the project backlog. How should it be handled?
options: As an exception to the board
test.why: A change that does not affect the project backlog is a detail change, handled informally at team level (11.3.2).

whyNot.0: Formal decisions by the board or change authority are for changes to the project baseline.
whyNot.2: Exceptions arise when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded, which is not the case here.
whyNot.3: An off-specification is a product that will not meet its specification; this is an improvement.

explain.body: Request for change: proposal to change a baseline. Off-specification: product will miss its specification. Problem: immediate negative impact. Business opportunity: unexpected positive consequence.

test.q: Larkspur Rail learns that Coinbridge Payments has gone into administration, putting the automatic payment work at immediate risk of stopping. Which type of issue is this?
test.why: A problem is an issue with an immediate negative impact, such as a supplier going bankrupt (11.3.1).

whyNot.0: No one is proposing a change to a baseline; the event itself is harming the project.
whyNot.1: No product has been found to miss its specification.
whyNot.3: A business opportunity is an unexpected positive consequence; this is negative.

explain.body: Trade items of similar effort, keep changes aligned with the project's goals, and agree the priority of both the new and the existing items with the product owner.

test.q: Easterholm County Council's digital team wants to add a newly requested story to the current sprint by trading. Which condition MOST matters for the trade to work as intended?
options: The story removed is of similar effort
The board approves the trade in advance
The new story is a Must have for the project
The trade is recorded in the risk register
test.why: Successful trading swaps requirements of similar effort, agreed with the PO, so the change is absorbed without increasing scope or disrupting the iteration (11.4.1).

whyNot.1: Trading within the project backlog is a team-level decision with the PO, not a board decision.
whyNot.2: Trading works with any priority level; what matters is similar effort and an agreed priority.
whyNot.3: The risk register records risks; a trade is a change to the product backlog agreed with the PO.

explain.body: First the team swarms on a blocker. If it cannot resolve it, the team escalates it as an issue to the project manager. It becomes an exception only if a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded.

test.q: Easterholm's digital team has swarmed for two days on a login fault but cannot fix it, because the cause lies in a council system the team cannot change. No tolerance is yet forecast to be exceeded. What should the team do NEXT?
options: Raise an exception report to the board
Trade the login story for one of equal effort
Escalate it as an issue to the project manager
Keep swarming until the stage boundary
test.why: If the team cannot resolve a blocker by swarming, it escalates it to the project manager as an issue; an exception is raised only if tolerances are forecast to be exceeded (11.4.2, Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, so an exception report is not yet needed.
whyNot.1: Trading absorbs changes in requirements; it does not resolve a blocker outside the team's control.
whyNot.3: The team has already tried swarming and cannot fix the cause, so it should escalate rather than wait.
